endorsements.quote: One of the first recommendations from our working group was creating a transparency label for AI-CDS systems called the Unique AI Identifier (UAII).

Information about training data and potential biases A comprehensive review of the data used to train the system, encompassing information on how and where it was obtained, population, location, care setting (if appropriate), and date range.
The UAII should enumerate any known limitations and warnings regarding domains of use, use cases, and any other information that could influence overall use or interpretations.
All systems should be revalidated after system or training data updates.
Regular review, calibration, and revalidation are necessary to correct drift and maintain accuracy.
A multi-layered approach should combine internal testing under varied use cases and ongoing monitoring (eg, using the UAII above label to complement adverse event reporting).
To ensure safe use of AI-CDS, there is a need for the creation of a National Healthcare AI-CDS Safety Reporting Clearinghouse.
As AI-CDS becomes mainstream, system- and tool-specific training of end users is critical for overall safe use, regardless of whether or not it resides inside otherwise familiar EHR systems.
Proper training should be clearly defined and repeated annually or in response to system updates and changes.

Our working group recommends creating a similar set of constructs and a parallel system for training requirements, which should be mandatory (depending on the application\u2019s envisioned end users\u2014for clinicians or laypeople) and documented and monitored as part of overall risk mitigation and legal/compliance constructs.
Such systems should be designed to provide user-friendly summaries for both clinicians and patients and support documentation encompassing: The goal and specific questions asked of the AI.

It is crucial to monitor and assess models, recommendations, and outcomes considering various forms of identity and social factors, such as race, socioeconomic status, health literacy, insurance coverage, etc.

This process includes early FDA dialogue, comprehensive clinical validation studies with RCTs, in-depth risk assessment and mitigation strategy development, detailed approval submission with all validation data and risk assessments, and post-market surveillance for monitoring real-world performance and identifying adverse events through continuous monitoring and reporting mechanisms.
Standard processes for conflict-of-interest disclosures should apply to all system developers.

unlisted_practices: Establish a finite certification period for AI-CDS systems, requiring review of the UAII and of use, performance, and adverse event data at expiration.
Standards development organizations should define specifications for required fields, formats, and APIs for AI-CDS data and metadata, and the UAII should be adapted as a FHIR class.
Regulators should mandate publication of the UAII transparency label to promote widespread adoption.
Cap AI-CDS autonomy levels by defining when, if ever, software may act without human confirmation.
Health professions educators should define AI-CDS competencies and incorporate them into medical education at all levels.
Developers should specify training requirements for users as part of the UAII process, with training and certification delivered by adult education experts.
Fund the AI-CDS safety reporting clearinghouse adequately and make reports part of the public record.
Select fairness metrics that align with the specific clinical purpose and use context-specific evaluation with stakeholder engagement.
Involve diverse, multidisciplinary stakeholders and a diverse workforce throughout the AI development lifecycle.
Disclose the version of the software, the data, and the training data in the UAII and refresh it on updates.
Regulators should develop more agile tools for near real-time review, re-evaluation, and certification of adaptive AI systems.

screen.reason: This is a consensus-derived recommendation framework paper from an AMIA/BIDMC working group providing guidelines and governance practices for AI-enabled clinical decision support systems.
